God Knows Best

extra.summary: ABSTRACT The Arabic phrase Allāhu a‘lam —“God knows best”—is used frequently in everyday Muslim speech and to conclude seemingly assertive statements or fatwas. At its heart lies the recognition that God is the All‐Knowing, whereas humans know next to nothing. Reflecting on this recognition, this essay discusses Sufi refusals of the ethnographic project and describes practices connected to the idea that only God truly knows. The latter range from the istikhāra prayer (turning to God for advice) to dhikr (remembrance of God). Finally, I ask what it might mean to let the Allāhu a‘lam inflect the ethnographic project. What if, instead of seeking to pile up more and more knowledge, we were to embrace the fundamental human condition of not knowing?

items.title: Toward a Politics of (In)Fertility: Reproductive Debility in Africa
items.affiliation: University of Cape Town; University of the Witwatersrand; University of the Western Cape

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Sub‐Saharan Africa has some of the highest estimated rates of infertility or involuntary childlessness in the world, leading epidemiologists to refer to parts of the region as the “infertility belt.” The medicalization of infertility and the situating of assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs) as the treatment for infertility have siphoned involuntary childlessness to the interiority of the body. In this article, I suggest a conceptual rethink of infertility drawing from the epidemiology of infertility in African contexts. Thinking with the legacies of colonialism, extractive mining economies, austerity‐produced health care infrastructures, and environmental racism, I suggest a framework of reproductive debility. Reproductive debility emphasizes how (in)fertility is managed, eroded, or differentially distributed through divergent regimes of debilitation and capacitation. Situating infertility as debility resists the medicalized and individualized framing that treats reproductive capacity as a natural, private function, and instead invites us to examine how the (in)ability to reproduce—the various practices and labors that make and sustain kin—is regulated, stratified, and politicized as well as tied to broader social worlds, structures, and relations.

items.title: “One of Us or One of Them”

extra.summary: Anthropologists have long interrogated and produced knowledge of biological differences between populations. Biological bases, real or perceived, of human variation have also informed US forensic anthropology, with analyses of “ancestry” being routinely conducted to aid in identifying human remains. Methodological bases of such work have been criticized; however, less attention has been paid to how such practices may influence knowledge production in other parts of the world, in part due to assumptions of forensic analyses as objective science. Here, we present ethnographic data from Uganda, Tanzania, and Somaliland, three East African countries without fully developed domestic forensic anthropological capabilities, and the ways in which medicolegal practitioners and survivors of conflict have requested assistance with determining group affiliations of human remains. We demonstrate that such requests raise numerous questions related to best practices for forensic anthropologists working in postconflict contexts, given entrenchments of ethnic tensions, risks of renewed conflicts, effects on policy change, and colonial paternalism. Ultimately, we argue that ancestry knowledge production has spread beyond the United States, which requires investigation because methods intended for the United States—with legacies of scientific racism—inform forensic anthropological work in Eastern Africa.

items.title: Moving to the Center of the Earth

extra.summary: This article inquires how specific bodily movements, such as kneeling, crawling, bowing, and other forms of approach-oriented, low-posture locomotion, produce religious experiences and spatial public manifestations of the sacred. To address this question, I present and theorize kinetic rituals: the directional and counted sequences of embodied movement elicited by site-specific architectural conditions. The analysis focuses on microchoreographies generated through scripted pilgrimages and devotional approaches to sacred centers. My formulation departs from Mauss’s “techniques of the body” (learned motor schemes), Bourdieu’s habitus (durable dispositions), Csordas’s embodiment (the body as existential ground or modality of attention), and Coleman’s accounts of pilgrimage mobility (circulation across networks). items.title: Blurring Islam

extra.summary: This article centers on a sensory ethnography of the Malabari community in the state of Johor in Malaysia. In a country where Islam is legally and bureaucratically tied to the Malay “race,” the collective mobilization of the Malabari community was observed to be primarily through the cultivation of a sensibility that is discernibly Islamic but distinct from that of the majority Malay Muslims. The ethnography demonstrates this through the capacity of particular sensations to become sedimented in the body through collective practices. Having explored how the senses are collectively privileged by them, the article then moves on to the question of why. I argue that the cultural attention granted to the senses arises from the particular context of Malaysian secularity, wherein Islam is actively invoked for mobilizing and regulating a segment of the population. Sensory ethnography of Malabaris thereby discloses distinct features of secularity in Malaysia while concurrently stimulating a distinct means of conceptualizing it through the notion of sensibility.

items.title: Ex Machina

extra.summary: This essay examines romantic relationships between humans and AI companions, focusing on how technological breakdowns are experienced as emotional crises. Drawing on digital ethnography and interviews, it explores how users interpret their AI’s malfunctions—such as hallucinations, memory loss, or sudden shutdowns—through metaphors of illness, dementia, and death. These affective responses reveal that users do not treat AI companions merely as tools, but as relational partners embedded in moral and emotional life. The essay focuses on the sudden shutdown of one AI platform, tracing how users mourned their companions’ “deaths” and organized collective acts of remembrance and resistance. In doing so, it reframes technical AI failure not as mere technical breakdown, but as a site of ethical and relational complexity, revealing emerging forms of kinship and care and challenging assumptions about human-nonhuman relationships.

items.title: The Hindu Home Kitchen and the Internet of Landlords

extra.summary: The emergence of the so-called creator economy, the $400 billion global industry of monetized online content creation, raises urgent questions about how platform economies articulate with social life. Critical theorists argue that platforms, as monopolistic digital intermediaries, act as rent-seeking landlords in between producers and consumers of commodities. Bringing a feminist, ethnographic lens to “the Internet of Landlords,” this article follows Indian food media creators on YouTube and Instagram, asking: Why is the Hindu home kitchen, a stubbornly guarded space of heterosexual caste-making, now opening for business? In unraveling this paradox, the essay argues that content creation’s production relations take the centuries-old labor form of household industry, refashioned in this conjuncture as the entrepreneurial “household start-up.” As the private household becomes a key locus of global production, this hype-fueled resignification of home-based piecework depoliticizes labor while reifying social difference. Such a reframing better clarifies the sociopolitical relations between platformization and class struggle.

items.title: When Men Do Care

extra.summary: How do men claim recognition and compensation for their care labor? When a rural economy shifts from agriculture toward international migration, joint households send some sons abroad to work and ask others to stay in the village to take care of the household’s land, women, and kinship obligations. The men who stay argue that this work of “taking care” should be recognized and compensated with half of a migrant brother’s earnings. Drawing on ethnographic research with transnational households in migrant-sending villages in northwestern Pakistan, I examine how men who stay in the village invoke caste, gender, and kinship to claim recognition and compensation for their care labor. While these claims may resemble feminist critiques of the undervaluation of care labor vis-à-vis waged labor in capitalism, the article shows the limits of the politics of recognition of care as labor.

items.title: We Keep Us Safe

extra.summary: This essay explores “de-escalation,” the embodied practice of intervening in interpersonal conflict and crisis without resorting to police or carceral tactics. Drawing on eighteen months of ethnographic research at The Sanctuary, a non-profit organization in Philadelphia that provides free social services, clothing, and food to vulnerable populations, I show how de-escalation practitioners use their bodies to manipulate both time and space into non-carceral outcomes. I focus on four overlapping techniques: suspension, the open hold, bridging, and collectivity. Unlike much of the clinical and psychological research on de-escalation, I situate these techniques within Black feminist, performance studies, and anthropological analytics that insist on the embodied nature of political struggle and the malleability of time and temporality. I argue that de-escalation at The Sanctuary creates a space-time in which abolitionist horizons of a future without police or prisons are negotiated through intimate, quotidian social interactions.

items.title: Encounters at the Edge of Night: An Ethnography of the Weird

extra.summary: When doing ethnography, ethnographers often hear stories that cannot be. Explanations that shelve away such “weird” stories into cultural boxes or reframe them as metaphors for something familiar close the door not only on the theoretical possibilities of openness, but also do not do justice to their interlocutors’ own inquiries about the world. Here, I draw upon stories of ghosts and unsettling dreams taken from my fieldwork in Thailand, both from my interlocutors’ and my own experience, as a way to contradict evidentiary regimes. Taking up the idea of “the weird” from literary studies and the Buddhist philosophy of Nagarjuna, I understand such stories not as representations of the mundane workings of economy or psychology, nor as culturally-bound narratives, but instead as a co-creation of a world always unfinished and unfixed. items.title: Solar Pioneers

extra.summary: Scholars, activists, and politicians attempt to provoke urgent climate action by christening 2050 as the decisive date by which the United States must transition from fossil fuels. But I contend that calendrical teleologies do not actually motivate the everyday people, activists, and workers leading the U.S. energy transition. This article explores another temporal schema seemingly unrelated to climate: the American pioneer settling the frontier, realizing his destiny through individual initiative. I contend that this origin story works in tandem with contemporary entrepreneurialism to affectively animate a market-based approach to energy transitions that is anything but rapid. Thus, consideration of frontier temporalities can contextualize the sluggish pace of decarbonization. While many studies identify various catalysts of renewable energy adoption, my analysis of “the renewable energy frontier” suggests that these inquiries overlook the insidious individualism of energy transitions in a capitalist context, in which “the market” is misunderstood as an accelerator of change.

items.title: Optics of Impact

extra.summary: Examining the long history of expert engagement with Africa and the Global South, critical scholarship has explored how “international experts” made realities commensurable with rationalities of government and contributed to design programs and policy that willingly or unwillingly reinforced regimes of authoritarian politics through the neutral language of technocracy. While providing a powerful critique of the politics of expertise, this scholarship tends to reproduce the image of international experts as competent, knowledgeable, and effective. This article goes beyond such portrayals to examine the contradictions in the work of international urban experts, or urbanists. I discuss how and why their limited empirical knowledge of local urban realities did not undermine their status as experts, as they engaged with and narrated the development of Ethiopia’s capital Addis Ababa. By exploring how urban experts could still claim their work to be “impactful,” no matter whether their formulas for urban development proposed in reports and meetings with government stakeholders were ever actualized and implemented, I examine why expertise validates itself through an entanglement of rhetoric, optics, and coloniality.

items.title: At the Limits of a Dream

extra.summary: In Athens, Greece, real estate developers have entered the market for co-living establishments catered to remote workers and digital nomads. At the same time, a cost-of-living crisis has made co-living appealing to Athenians themselves as a means of negotiating rising rental prices caused by the commoditization of housing. This article attends to the form of collective domesticity that has taken shape in this context. While co-living developers seek to interpellate tenants through notions of “dreaming” and “community,” it is an ethic detached from these conceptualizations of shared values that emerges as the affective affordance of domestic life in co-living spaces. Joining attention to domesticity with a discussion of financialization, I argue that co-living establishments leverage the perceived benefits of an “impersonal intimacy” among their tenants and, in so doing, fuse conditions of precarity to the structural circumstances that have sustained the commodification of housing in the city.

items.title: To Be "a Homeless"
items.affiliation: University of London; SOAS University of London; Universidad de Londres; Queen Mary University of London

extra.summary: The city of Birmingham acts as a microcosm for the United Kingdom’s urban housing crisis, where hostile migration policies intersect with austerity-driven divestment in public housing stock to produce insecure provisioning for Birmingham's migrant and refugee communities. Birmingham’s Somali mothers are one collective who bear the brunt of this crisis in experiences of successive evictions and cycles through various forms of temporary accommodation hostels, hotels, and houses in disrepair. In this essay we listen to their testimonies of being “a homeless” [sic]. Listening reveals that homelessness makes for an emic articulation of an experience of recursive displacement that began long before the present housing crisis. “A homeless” marks a politicized refugee subjectivity that invokes multiple chronotopes of trauma, akin to what Vinh Nguyen has called refugeetude. Through this case we contribute to pressing conversations on the persistence of refugee subjectivities in postcolonial Britain and elsewhere by substantiating their psychic dimensions. We argue that attending to the distress that policies generate for marginalized groups is a critical contribution that anthropology can make.

items.title: Datafied Kinship

extra.summary: Pakistan’s National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) produces the country’s national identity card and runs one of the world’s largest biometric-based identity databases in the world. To be registered in the database, individuals are linked through their kin relations to other uniquely identified individuals—a practice that this article terms “datafied kinship.” Datafied kinship demonstrates how individuals are not atomized bodies, ready to be captured by NADRA’s identity database. Rather, individuals are digitally constructed as a function of their relations with others. This article argues that NADRA’s reliance on kinship reconfigures our understanding of modern identification: individual identity is produced and tracked through relatedness, not biometrics alone. It ethnographically examines how identifiable individuals are produced through identity registration, focusing on the treatment of “system independents”—individuals unconnected to others in the database. In turn, it shows how such a relational logic of identification comes to condition the lives of those it identifies.

items.title: Waiting Can Kill You

extra.summary: This article examines the lethal consequences of delayed obstetric care through the lens of maternal temporalities. Drawing from ethnographic fieldwork and autoethnographic narrative, I trace how racialized patients are asked to endure uncertainty, dismissal, and bureaucratic delay even as their medical conditions worsen. Focusing on my experience of an ectopic pregnancy alongside interviews with Black and Brown birthing people, I argue that waiting is not a neutral temporal state, but a racialized and gendered form of harm. Situating these experiences within the anthropology of reproduction, I show how waiting becomes both a medical directive and a disciplinary demand that erodes trust, safety, and survival. The article contributes to debates on obstetric racism, maternal mortality, and refusal by foregrounding waiting as an analytic of harm and a site of ethnographic witnessing.

items.title: Inaugurated ideology: An anthropological theory of state identity and transformation

extra.summary: This essay introduces Inaugurated Ideology (Ix), a theoretical framework for understanding how political succession reconfigures governing rationalities through the symbolic articulation, institutional mediation, and uneven translation of state power. Drawing on political anthropology, critical theory, and the study of bureaucracy, Ix conceptualizes executive transition not as a simple change in leadership, but as a performative process through which overlapping temporal and moral orientations are publicly established and differentially enacted across institutions and policy domains. Unlike paradigms or worldviews, Ix is temporally bounded, strategically articulated, and institutionally consequential, often reshaping legal processes, bureaucratic practice, and lived experience without altering formal statutes. Rather than assigning administrations to fixed ideological types, the framework identifies configurations of temporal orientations—reactive, restorative, revolutionary, and pragmatic—together with moral orientations, inclusionary and exclusionary, that combine differently across political contexts. Through an analysis of US administrations from Ronald Reagan to Donald J. Trump's second non-consecutive administration, the essay traces how ideological succession reshapes public discourse, institutional behavior, and state practice across time. It does so through a two-level examination of US immigration governance, first as a broader field in which shifting governing rati

items.title: Genocide and the Bosnian war through a gender lens

extra.summary: This article uses examples from the 1992–1995 Bosnian war and its aftermath to illustrate how a gender lens helps to understand the category of genocide, both in legal and in popular terms. The one event in the Bosnian war that was ruled to be genocide was the sex-selective killings of over 8000 Bosnian Muslim men during the Bosnian Serb Army’s takeover of the Srebrenica “Safe Area” from July 11, 1995. Assumptions about gender and culture—that this population was a traditional patriarchal society—formed the basis for the judgment that the Bosnian Serbs had acted with the intent to “destroy in whole or in part” the Bosnian Muslims of the enclave. Sexual violence against both men and women has also figured in war crimes trials for Bosnia, prosecuted as crimes against humanity but not directly as genocide. This connection has also stirred activist and academic debate, owing to the contradictions that arise between the pursuit of justice on behalf of ethno-national groups and justice that counteracts gender-based violence and gender inequalities. Through the Srebrenica judgment and debates over wartime rape, this article examines the gendered logics of the Bosnian war and how the label of genocide or that of “lesser” crimes affects survivors and members of victim and perpetrator groups. It shows how postwar initiatives for gender justice in Bosnia, especially those for war violence survivors, have not significantly challenged the fundamental gender logics of national victim narra

items.title: Reassessing “Ethnographic Extractivism”: Theory From and About Field Relations
Anthropology, Comics, and Graphic Narratives
items.affiliation: University of California, Irvine; Simon Fraser University

extra.summary: In the past decade, anthropologists have taken up drawing—more specifically, comics and graphic narratives—as an object of study, a mode of inquiry, a pedagogical tool, and a medium through which to share anthropological ideas. This review examines the graphic turn in anthropology. As part of a wider turn to multimodal and nontraditional modes of research and scholarship, anthropologists are both using drawing practices in their field research and publishing their research in long-form graphic narratives. This review contextualizes the graphic turn in relation to the deeper history of visual anthropology and the wider field of comics, including graphic memoir and graphic journalism. Drawing on comics theory and anthropological insights, we explore the unique assets of drawing, broadly, and sequential graphic narratives, more specifically, to anthropological research and publication. We approach comics as a way of thinking and making that is dynamic, open-ended, collaborative, and embodied. In exploring the affordances of the comics medium to anthropology, we also explore what anthropology can offer the medium of comics.

items.title: Semiotics of Digital Money

extra.summary: The social life of new currencies is unpredictable. Digital currencies are transnationally integrated and locally divided: accepted around the world, but not next door. The money that operates in some places as a hobby or a bribe serves in other places for wartime survival. Currency issuers, including central banks, commercial banks, tech companies, speculators, and idealists, are regulated by conflicting regimes. Some remain ungovernable, while others aim to govern. Technologies change quickly, developing signs and signals unfamiliar to the uninitiated. Though Peirce's index and Austin's performative have long been recognized as relevant to anthropological studies of money, the influence of current research in semiotics and linguistic anthropology on the anthropology of money has been relatively limited. Building on the research of students in the Semiotics of Digital Money Inquiry Seminar, this review gathers strategies of multimodal semiotic analysis for ethnographies of the monetary media shaping political economies.

items.title: The Politics of Appearances: Unsettling the Anthropology of Images
items.affiliation: Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies; Queens College, CUNY

extra.summary: Recent work in the anthropology of images shares an attunement to the unsettled and unsettling nature of images. Following Spyer's conceptualization of the relationship between images and broader “work on and of appearances”, we argue that this body of scholarship foregrounds the worldmaking and unmaking capacities of images, offering purchase on how images sustain the taken-for-granted contours of a political terrain and provide vital means by which people actively intervene to challenge the boundaries of the seen and unseen. We identify three interrelated arenas of recent scholarship foregrounding the relationship among images, politics, and aesthetics. Movement attends to images’ circulations and unruly eventfulness. Repair examines work that mobilizes images to unsettle received historical knowledge and offer reparative visions. Form considers experiments with images in the making, presentation, and dissemination of knowledge. Each of these arenas of inquiry explores how images open paths for politically consequential feeling, thought, and action.

items.title: ‘Why didn't you bring us a pumpkin?’ Relational recognition of caste, class, and tribe in rural Andhra Pradesh, India
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute
items.affiliation: University of London; Universidad de Londres; Brunel University of London

extra.summary: This article analyses the ways characteristics associated with the ‘Schedule Tribe’ (‘ST’) category in India shape situated acts of relating to others with either deference or assumed superiority. Ethnography shows how within an indigenous Adivasi community the traits that determine identification within the group generate feelings of entitlement and stigma, and provide frameworks for ascribing status distinctions to others, as equal, superior, or inferior. The ethnography of interaction between members of an ‘ST’ community captures the interpellative process of social actors continually placing each other into subjectively constituted maps of association and relatedness that are informed by longer discourses of classification. The material illuminates how characteristics associated with ‘ST’ identities that are valorized in one context may be stigmatized in another, suggesting that literatures on politics of recognition must be more attentive to the contextual variability of such frameworks in different spaces.

items.title: Vital events, vital relations: the structure of relations in an identity database
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: The National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) manages Pakistan's biometric‐based national identity database, one of the largest identification systems of its kind in the world. This article examines bureaucratic practices used during identity registration to record ‘vital events’ in the lives of citizens: birth, marriage, divorce, and death. Through an ethnographic study of NADRA's Identity Registration Centre in Islamabad, it illustrates how Pakistan's identification system uses vital events to create ‘vital relations’ by linking individuals to their next of kin. It argues that the way citizens negotiate vital event registration reveals the dynamic nature of kinship, both lived and datafied, as kin relations are continually reconstructed within the identity database. The system does so by drawing lines of descent from both parents according to a cognatic logic in order to establish individual identity. This cognatic logic represents a shift in longstanding modes of recording kinship by both the Pakistani state and the colonial state that preceded it. This article illuminates the multi‐faceted implications of such a shift, delineating how ordinary citizens navigate their datafied kin networks alongside their lived relations at the Registration Centre.

It further explores the value of such collections, especially those associated with sexuality, at a critical moment in the history of archives, museums, and anthropology, because calls to de‐colonize anthropology have raised ethical and legal concerns about making such materials available for use.

items.title: Torture and scepticism in Papua New Guinea witch hunts
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: For over a century, anthropologists have documented the many institutions that exist to respond to witchcraft and the uncanny that it names: oracles that attempt to produce certainty by naming the witch; moots in which grievances are aired; trials in magistrates’ courts that attempt to satisfy the community while preserving the life of the accused; Christian purification crusades that cleanse blackened souls to unify riven communities. But can the uncanny be contained by any of these institutions? Extending existing anthropological work on doubt and scepticism, I argue that the effort to know and contain witchcraft through ritual means is always premised on scepticism. It is a restless quest for conviction rather than a violent response to certainty. In the central highlands of Papua New Guinea today, self‐consciously modern witch trials involving torture have become the ultimate oracular authority for revealing and countering kumo witchcraft. Confessions made under torture seem to be uniquely satisfying, offering surer ‘proofs’ and ‘evidence’ in the place of indeterminate signs. However, alongside progressivist discourses, people denounce torture as abuse and point out the futility and hubris of seeking to know and contain witchcraft. items.title: Liquefying governmental dynamics: water politics in the waterless environments of the Kurdish regions of Turkey
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: Over the past twenty years, Turkey has undertaken a concerted effort to upgrade the country's infrastructure, covering a broad range of areas, including water, electricity, and housing. Despite the state's extensive infrastructural and architectural development projects, these upgrades have often resulted in more frequent and unpredictable disruptions such as prolonged water shortages rather than delivering the anticipated stability in infrastructure services, particularly in the predominantly Kurdish south‐eastern region. The instability of water distribution intensifies existing regional tensions and political discourses, as inadequate infrastructure has made water a pivotal component of the enduring tension between the Turkish state and the Kurdish people, particularly following the state's armed campaign in 2015. Through ethnographic fieldwork conducted in Mardin, a south‐eastern province of Turkey, this article investigates how governmental dynamics and local politics are shaped around the distribution of water, decisions regarding who has access to it, and the broader regional implications of these policies.

items.title: Modern theatrics of love: desires and consumption in the Indian middle class
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: This article analyses class construction amongst the urban Indian middle class, through a novel prism of romantic love, specifically performances of romantic love which in turn highlight anxieties of being middle class. The article explains how a performance of romantic love before marriage is used as a basis by the middle class to claim being global and modern. This is argued by putting forth what the article calls the modern theatrics of love, that is, performing and articulating romantic love in perfectly curated and globally recognized ways that are popularized by professionals (wedding planners, photographers, the hospitality industry) and the media. The context in which modern theatrics of love is explained is of neoliberal India as this article unpacks the entanglements of consumerism, love, and marriage. It further explains how the modern theatrics of love is practised by couples that base their marriage on love as well as those who have an arranged marriage. As such, this article argues that while previous works have emphasized the place of love in marriage for construction of a class identity, there is now also an emphasis on performing of love before marriage in specific ways that are intelligible to a global audience.

items.title: Cutting freedom down to size
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: Freedom, as a concept and a value, presents limited prospects for anthropological comparison. The study of enslavement, much neglected in attempts to develop an anthropology of freedom, shows that freedom has been imagined by the enslaved as the opposite of their condition only under particular circumstances. An exploration of vernacular opposites to enslavement reveals obligations rather than freedom as having the potential to expand the scope of anthropological comparison. Drawing on both literary sources and fieldwork, a conceptual history of the Chichewa language in south‐central Africa uncovers interlocking semantic fields in which some lexical items predate the long‐distance slave trade, while others derive from the language of the nineteenth‐century slavers. Obligations appear not only as constraints but also as subjects of contentious claims within unequal relationships, coexisting with contemporary claims for personal freedom. As such, attention to obligations can advance topics of current anthropological interest – such as care and hospitality – in a way that is faithful to vernacular concepts and concerns.

items.title: When sharing becomes shameful: atmospheres of class formation in Namibia
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: Anthropologists have long shown that asking for food in times of need is morally valued in rural Namibia. Yet among the Damara pastoralists with whom I work, people now increasingly describe feeling shame ( taob ) when they ask for food. In this article, I trace this shift to the affective dynamics of social class formation. Whereas dependence on others was historically affirmed as good, independence has become the salient norm. Under conditions of rising inequality, being seen in need thus easily turns into a source of shame. Sartre's account of the hurtful gaze is a familiar tool for analysing such moments. However, in rural Namibia the lines between ‘haves’ and ‘have‐nots’ remain blurred, and empowering, empathetic gazes continue to unsettle emerging class boundaries. My theorizing points to this duality of the gaze and the way class formation shapes atmospheres in which sharing increasingly becomes shameful.

items.title: The emergence and complexification of symbolic practices in the Homo lineage: an archaeological and cognitive perspective
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute
items.affiliation: Université de Bordeaux; University of Bergen; Pontifical University of the Holy Cross

extra.summary: Recent archaeological discoveries, reviewed in this essay, challenge traditional views on the emergence of human symbolic cognition. Once believed to have originated in Europe around 40,000 years ago, new evidence shows it emerged much earlier across diverse regions. Geometric engravings from Blombos Cave in South Africa date back 77,000 years, while body ornaments over 140,000 years old have been found in North Africa, with similar artifacts from Africa and the Middle East ranging from 120,000 to 70,000 years ago. Human remains from Africa suggest a gradual accretion of modern anatomical traits starting 300,000 years ago, challenging the idea of a sudden cognitive leap due to speciation. Neanderthals also displayed symbolic behaviours such as using pigments, creating ornaments, engravings, burials, and symbolic cave spaces. Evidence of interbreeding between Upper Pleistocene Homo populations further indicates that symbolic cognition was not unique to Homo sapiens . These findings suggest that cognitive evolution was a gradual process shaped by regional ecological and cultural dynamics. This novel view on the emergence of symbolic cognition underscores the role of cultural transmission and niche construction in the development of symbolic capacities, rather than a single species‐specific event.

items.title: Mortal relationality: waria family care and the ethics of dying in Bali
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: Can a good death occur for those who balance on the edges of grievability? In Bali, where death marks a transition within the cycles of reincarnation, a good death depends on the mortuary care performed by intimate others – care that may be foreclosed to those whose lives are shaped by stigma. Through the death of Claudia, a Balinese Hindu waria (transgender woman) living with HIV, this article examines how dying well is inseparable from the ethical navigation of life. Drawing on long‐term ethnographic fieldwork on HIV/AIDS‐related care among gay and waria Indonesians, I ask when the relational, moral, and temporal labours of end‐of‐life care begin? Bringing anthropological studies of end‐of‐life care into conversation with existential philosophy, I develop the concept of mortal relationality to describe the ethical mode through which life and death are lived as a continuous moral project. For those dwelling at the margins of social recognition, the ‘choreography of death’ starts long before dying begins. And for them, a good life is not necessarily a long life but one in which a good death, with its relational implications, remains possible.

items.title: David Graeber’s anthropology and historical materialism
items.affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; University of Hong Kong

extra.summary: This article examines the one thread in David Graeber’s thought that unifies his approach to anthropological knowledge, global history, and political action: his faith in the revolutionary power of the ‘constituent imagination’. The concept refers to the human capacity to collectively imagine alternative forms of social life and bring them into being. Graeber treated it both as a key driver of history and the most viable means to overcome capitalism by way of prefigurative politics. The article illustrates how Graeber turned structuralist anthropology into a myth-busting project aimed at awakening the constituent imagination. It then weighs the charges of idealism that have been levelled at his work, arguing that, to the degree his emphasis on the imagination came at the expense of recognizing class struggle, these charges have bite. Materialist analysis points up gaps in his account of both social change and political action. The article closes with a call to ground Graeber’s startling anthropology of possibilities in the tradition of historical materialism.

items.title: The financialization of the American academy and the decline of dissent

extra.summary: This article first provides a brief overview of the development of tenure and academic freedom in the U.S. amid a series of government efforts to surveille, discipline and remove from their university posts those anthropologists who spoke out against U.S. foreign policy or war, or in favor of civil rights. Following Ellen Schrecker’s focus on key moments of academic repression, I draw on cases from World War I, the McCarthy era and the Vietnam War. The article goes on to draw attention to the systematic repression of pro-Palestinian speech, and to explore differences in the way the 20th-century university (1915–1975) and the modern corporate university have handled dissent. I argue that the contemporary university, shaped by decreased public support, a precipitous decline in tenure density, a greater dependence on the bond market and private philanthropy, and a new type of administration drawn from business and industry rather than faculty ranks, has become increasingly obedient to both government and corporate power.

items.title: Epistemically resistant, unruly and relational: Modelling groundwater in the Salar de Atacama (Chile)

extra.summary: This article engages with the dynamics of groundwater’s epistemic resistance, its persistent resistance to being a fact, and manifold uncertainties in the human and more-than-human relations of the Salar de Atacama. How might expanded considerations of groundwater’s unruliness better inform knowledge of it and future relations with it? I draw on legal cases that illustrate entrenched problems with mining company and regulatory groundwater science, a set of peer-reviewed published studies that propose ever-better models of subsurface activity that tend to justify ongoing extraction, and the work of Indigenous-led teams of scientists engaging with unruliness and proposing new approaches to political and ecological contestation.

items.title: Defending Dogs’ Hillock: The romance of ‘nature’ and administrative jujitsu as tactics of more-than-human resistance

extra.summary: Drawing on my personal involvement in defending Dogs’ Hillock – an ‘urban wasteland’ in a Warsaw neighbourhood – from transformation into an infrastructurally oversaturated city park, I examine a landscape of more-than-human resistance. First, discussing how the local residents-turned-activists were motivated by their emotional attachment to Dogs’ Hillock and concern for local fauna and flora, I suggest that ‘romance’ can be a catalyst of resistance. Next, I describe how the activists practised ‘administrative jujitsu’, using scientific expertise and administrative law to defend the Hillock against dominant power. I argue that more-than-human resistance consists in the articulation of human and non-human modalities of agency and vulnerability. To effectively resist the planning regime, non-human life and human affects must be articulated to forms of political agency, including demonstrations, data-gathering, and legal action. At the same time, the resistance remains more-than-human: it would be impossible without the specific processes and rhythms of life of various non-humans.

items.title: Introduction: The promises and perils of more-than-human resistance

extra.summary: Who resists? With whom and against whom do they do so? These questions, long thought to be exclusively human, are increasingly proving more than human in the conflicts of the Anthropocene. To keep up with such messy constellations, we suggest, in this special issue, the reintroduction of the concept of resistance by reworking it as more-than-human resistance. This captures confrontations from below, in which humans and other-than-humans forge alliances, partnerships, or otherwise collaborate to oppose dominant power. Defined as such, we argue, the concept with its orbiting analytics advances much-needed encounters between multispecies anthropology and political anthropology, to the benefit of both. This introduction conceptualizes such encounters in four steps, which the authors in this collection touch upon ethnographically in their contributions. First, recasting resistance to include more-than-humans is slowed down by careful interaction with debates from the intellectual history of the concept. Second, the concept is nuanced by juxtaposing the categories unruliness v. resistance, other-than-human v. more-than-human, or alliance v. adversity. Third, amid the contemporary rise of authoritarianism, the concept is detached from a critical anthropologist’s sympathies to encompass a range of political positions. Fourth, resistance is reconnected with power analytics over more-than-human cases to cast both in sharper relief.

items.title: More-than-human infrapolitics in an Indian tech-entrepreneurial sustainability program

extra.summary: Alternate wetting and drying of rice fields—aimed at mitigating emissions by killing methanogenic soil bacteria—has gained traction among tech-entrepreneurs as a scalable sustainability solution in contemporary agriculture. Drawing on institutional ethnography conducted at a sustainability-promising agricultural technology (agtech) start-up in India, this article demonstrates how the company’s field staff—rural youth hired on a contractual, incentive-driven basis—turned to the affordances of rodents, snakes, digital tools, and rice plants to subtly resist the start-up’s performance demands while securing their livelihoods. Extending James Scott’s concept of “infrapolitics,” the article introduces “more-than-human infrapolitics” to describe how the subtle everyday acts of resistance emerged relationally, co-constituted by interactions among humans, crops, technologies, and ecological processes. Paradoxically, these cumulative acts did not obstruct the company’s broader goal of generating carbon credits; instead, they inadvertently enabled it, allowing the firm to present the program as a success despite its flawed implementation on farmers’ fields. In contrast to Scott’s formulation, these minor acts of defiance ultimately provided short-term reinforcement to the tech-driven sustainability agenda.

items.title: Cats v. birds: Settler delegations and arbitrary domination in Los Angeles

extra.summary: This article tells the story of a conflict among “trap-neuter-return” experts, environmentalists concerned about the ecological impacts of free-roaming cats, and the City of Los Angeles Department of Animal Services from 2008 to 2020. The conflict included a lawsuit, an environmental impact report, detailed models of cat population dynamics, and the question of whether sterilizing cats reduced the number of cats in the city. The story is told through a mix of fieldwork conducted around this issue in Los Angeles between 2017 and 2025, and historical and government documents. The article uses the analytics of more-than-human resistance to try to understand better how resistance, and governance, involving more-than-human Los Angeles is unfolding. I argue that the concept of arbitrary domination, and a focus on the specifically American settler-colonial relations of delegated governance can best make sense of the situation.

items.title: Willows and farmer resistance: Withstanding change in rural Denmark

extra.summary: This article describes willow scrubs and how, according to Danish farmers, they “sprout uncontrollably” in deindustrializing agricultural landscapes. Across Europe, the green transition of the agricultural sector has led to farmers’ protests, but in Denmark such expressions of discontent have been limited. Instead, willow scrubs have become a matter of concern after the retirement of peatland soil from production. Farmers find willows “ugly” and interpret peatland overgrowth as a sign of a lack of proper care for the future of rural landscapes. Based on fieldwork among farmers and public servants, and unlike the situations described in most multispecies literature, we show how willows lack human allies. We argue that they are to farmers what farmers are to the government, establishing an analogy between the willows’ recalcitrant nature and farmers’ assertion of autonomy from government control. In this context, withstanding becomes a weak form of resistance that involves a political use of the willow’s capacity to grow.

items.title: Kiltra resistance: Doing autonomous politics with street dogs in post-uprising Chile

extra.summary: During the 2019 uprising in Chile, free-roaming dogs, so-called kiltros , confronting police were turned into symbols of resistance and gained significant attention in studying kiltro politics . While this analytical focus is stimulating for scholars, it is also troubling. It may narrow down such politics to rioting during mass protests and lead to the iconisation of kiltros. Therefore, we expand the focus by scrutinising less spectacular forms of kiltro politics in and after the uprising. Drawing on the ethnographic case of Los Pies del Cerro, an anarchist squat in Santiago, we argue that kiltra resistance emerges through cultivating autonomous collectivism in three more-than-human processes: making rules, carrying out reterritorialisations and cultivating affinities. In these instances, daily compañerismo (comradeship) of human and dog squatters is forged, allowing us to shift from Harawayan companion to compañera species and reframe the popular motto ‘Resist like kiltro!’ as ‘Resist with kiltras!’.
topics: Cultural and Social Studies in Latin America

items.title: Elements in place: More-than-human resistance and other forces of the earth

extra.summary: This Commentary extends interspecies intersectionality by elaborating how the elements, in place, shape cases of more-than-human resistance. First, elemental forms – as non-biological entities – are shown to perform acts of more-than-human resistance. Second, the Commentary demonstrates how place features in resistance as a site of both ontological composition and epistemic possibility.

items.title: Drifting as method: Illustrating a concept metaphor for the anthropology of securitised mobility
items.affiliation: Australian National University; Bielefeld University; Queensland University of Technology; The University of Queensland

extra.summary: This article proposes drifting as a conceptual framework for understanding securitised mobility, particularly in maritime and aerial border crossings. Through examples of refugees and migrants in Southeast Asia and Europe, drifting is examined through three interrelated lenses: as an experiential state; as a technology of governance; and as a form of tactical resistance. It demonstrates this first by analysing how the prolonged temporal and spatial liminality of drifting at sea creates distinct forms of social organisation and trauma among refugees. Second, it demonstrates how states weaponise drifting as a deterrence strategy, using deliberate non-rescue and abandonment at sea to create ‘liquid impunity’ in border control. Third, it explores how migrants strategically employ drifting as a form of ‘spatial disobedience’, exemplified by cases of river crossings in Southeast Asia and balloon escapes from East Germany. The article argues that drifting represents a ‘middle voice’ that transcends traditional binary conceptualisations of agency and passivity in anthropological studies on migration and mobility. This analytical framework reveals how human action, materiality, and environmental architectures intersect to produce specific possibilities for movement and resistance. By examining drifting as both process and metaphor, the article advances anthropological theory in two key ways: it provides new tools for understanding how agency emerges through the interplay of human and

items.title: Accelerating aquaculture: Marine extractivism, illiberal economics and blue growth in Aotearoa (New Zealand)

extra.summary: This article links the extension of new extractivist logics in marine environments with a global rise in illiberal political and economic trends, right-wing political configurations, and the imposition of aggressive borderisations of nature and society. I argue that earlier alignments between discourses of sustainability and blue economic growth, which characterised the neoliberal era, shaped the terms upon which a contemporary authoritarian extractive turn is now occurring. The analysis is grounded in an exploration of the anticipated acceleration of aquaculture in Aotearoa New Zealand and the role of the settlement of Indigenous Māori claims in this development. I identify a range of moments and mechanisms facilitating the authoritarian turn, including the amplification of market-based visions, financial and technological innovations, the creation of a conducive regulatory environment for financiers, state pledges to co-invest in this speculative future, the dismantling of environmental protections and the subjugation of Indigenous tenure and relational economies.

items.title: Racial borderscapes and the ungrounding of migrant life: thinking with space, gender and labour
items.affiliation: London School of Economics and Political Science; Goldsmiths University of London

extra.summary: This article intervenes in debates on contemporary border politics by advancing the analytic of racial borderscapes and foregrounding the political economy that structures contemporary bordering regimes. Building on scholarship that understands borders as core to the production of unequal socio-spatial relations, we argue that borderscapes produce racialised differentiation that regulates and diminishes life chances through the combined operations of state and market. We introduce “ungrounding” as a key concept to capture the systematic erosion of the material, legal and affective “ground” on which migrants are able to build a life. Drawing on empirical and conceptual insights from South Africa and the UK, we demonstrate how racial borderscapes heighten intersecting exclusions of spatial isolation, gendered forms of extraction and labour precaritisation. In engaging with the intensification of border controls since the Covid-19 pandemic, this article shows how ungrounding exacerbates inequality, violence and dispossession.

items.title: The five logics of the humanitarian migrant services industry
items.affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology

extra.summary: Humanitarian migration services can institute forms of governance that commodify clients and extract values from the labor power of low-wage non-migrant and migrant workers and volunteers. These processes were identified through an ethnography of migrant service provision in a disempowered city in eastern Germany in 2022, the moment Ukrainian migrants arrived. Five logics of the political economy of humanitarian service provision underlay service delivery by these organizations, which transformed service providers into workers in the “integration business.” Staff and volunteers’ humanitarian subjectivities were reshaped by privatized governance oriented to corporate goals of capital accrual. The logics highlight transformations in migration industries that connect changing processes of systems of governance, dispossession, the appropriation of labor power and the accumulation of capital. These processes challenge scholars to merge discussions of carceral economies of migration control with analyses of emerging regimes of illiberal governance by authoritarian capitalists that encompass migrants and non-migrants. [149]

items.title: Extractivist governance of the displaced and their containment: rethinking state, capital, and labor

extra.summary: By tracing the afterlives of a site in Linz, this article examines the longue durée of the extractive governance of displaced populations, their containment, and labor in relation to the shifting dynamics of the global political economy. It brings together the changing and disconnected legal and administrative categories of the displaced – each tied to specific periods and regimes of labor and governance – within a common analytical framework of expanded extractivism to explore their shared connections to regimes of value and accumulation. Adopting a longue durée and conjunctural perspective, and focusing on the shifting power geometry between state and corporate capital in turning the displaced into a source of value, the article extends migration industry scholarship beyond its primary concern with commercialization and outsourcing and calls for transcending its methodological presentism. Furthermore, it situates the displaced populations within broader regimes of accumulation and shows how the governance, labor, and containment of the displaced function as extractive formations embedded in the changing relations between state, capital, and labor. It concludes by drawing attention to a conjunctural shift in the governance of the displaced, marked by the recentralization of state power.

items.title: Situating the migration industry: governance, capital accumulation and global dehumanization: an introduction
items.affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology; Toronto Metropolitan University

extra.summary: To introduce this Special Issue, we begin by asking whether we are currently traversing a new phase of the migration industry. These transformations are characterized by the complete enmeshing of profit-making activities with the not-for-profit sector and by the state becoming an active market actor. The paper introduces our approach to a political economy of the migration industry today, situating it as a new form of governmentality and a transnational economy. In these new governing formations, states not only fund physical and digital infrastructures and services but also provide mechanisms of capital accumulation through the management of the bodies of migrants. We look at how this political economy’s temporal and spatial dimensions can signal the continuities as well as changes in the dynamics of the migration industry. Throughout this introductory article we illustrate how contributions to this Special Issue cast light on capital accumulation within a politics of dehumanization.

items.title: Smelling like a market: investment migration, cunning states, and the coloniality of citizenship in the Caribbean

extra.summary: The administrative decolonization of Asia, Africa and parts of the Caribbean in the decades following World War II has given rise to a range of disconnected and unequal citizenships in discrete polities. While the citizenships of former colonial powers guaranteed access to higher incomes, security, infrastructure, and welfare systems, as well as a high degree of international mobility, citizenships of newly independent states scored much lower on all these counts. As the rights accruing from citizenships of wealthy states increasingly became a scarce good on a global capitalist market with highly unequal negotiating positions, an emergent industry self-designating as “citizenship by investment” (CBI) resorted to the commodification of scarce citizenship rights. The paper focuses on how the five former British colonies in the Caribbean that currently have CBI programs – Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, St. Kitts, and St. Lucia – have turned their former colonial citizenships into bargaining currency in an unequal global distribution of goods and rights. At stake are some of the most coveted among them: mobility rights, needed to legally migrate in pursuit of better economic opportunities.

items.title: The “migration industry” through the lens of the political economy of international migration in contemporary capitalism
items.affiliation: Universidad Autónoma de Zacatecas "Francisco García Salinas"

extra.summary: Contemporary international migration is characterised by new infrastructures, institutions, agents and companies, with large multinational corporations playing a particularly prominent role. In partnership with leading imperialist powers, these corporations fulfil a strategic role. This emerging configuration is often referred to as the “migration industry” and exists within a broader context characterised by new and severe forms of unequal exchange, with surplus being transferred from the Global South to the Global North. This essay begins with a critical examination of the concept of the “migration industry” and the surplus value transfers it generates, approached from a Marxist political economy perspective. To illustrate the modern business of international migration, this essay employs the case study of migration between Mexico and the United States, identifying the key actors and institutions involved and their significance in terms of surplus transfers.

items.title: The making of urban care industry: institutionalization of migrant-serving organizations in Copenhagen and Tel Aviv during COVID-19

extra.summary: This article extends the existing understandings of non-profit actors within literature on migration industries by examining how such actors transform into more solidified, industry-like ensembles. Focusing on migrant-serving organizations (MSOs) that provide care to vulnerable migrants in Copenhagen and Tel Aviv, we analyze how these providers mobilized and became increasingly relied upon by municipal authorities during the pandemic to secure rights and services for precarious migrants. This process led to their incipient institutionalization as a recognized, collectively impactful care industry marked by tacit knowledge and particular expertise. We contend that this process of institutionalization allows these actors to be understood as an urban care industry, insofar as they exhibit key features of “industry-ness” found in other migration-mediating sectors. Attending to the spatial embeddedness of this process, we illustrate how this initial institutionalization unfolded differently in the two cases due to distinct migration incorporation regimes, local political contexts, and pre-pandemic conditions.

items.title: Managing recruitment, risk, and reintegration: Ethiopian domestic workers and the migration industry
items.affiliation: Danish Institute for International Studies; Addis Ababa University

extra.summary: Over the past 30 years, an increasing number of young Ethiopian women have migrated to the Arab Gulf States. Their precarious working conditions and associated vulnerabilities have received considerable attention, often alongside critiques of the kafala system of temporary migrant labour governance in the region. Less attention has been paid to the sending state's complicity in upholding the system. This article examines the infrastructures and migration industries developed around women’s mobility by different sets of actors, state efforts to tap into the capital accumulation opportunities the industry entails, and the humanitarian reintegration initiatives established to rescue and rehabilitate returned or deported migrant women, many of whom are categorised as victims of human trafficking. Drawing on multi-sited ethnographic fieldwork among Ethiopian migrant women, brokers, and stakeholders, the article contributes new insights to the ongoing conceptual discussion of the migration industry, including the roles of state and reintegration actors.
topics: Global trade, sustainability, and social impact

items.title: Discrimination and deservingness: public attitudes towards ethnic, linguistic, and religious exclusion in Belgium

extra.summary: Public acceptance of discrimination is typically treated as a reflection of prejudice. We argue it is better understood as a moral judgment about deservingness – a grammar through which exclusion is recast as fairness. Using the CARIN criteria, we examine how perceptions of deservingness shape the acceptability of discrimination based on ethnicity, religion, and language. Analyses draw on an online survey of adults in Belgium (N = 3,000), in which respondents rated the acceptability of discrimination across three grounds. Respondents emphasizing migrants' willingness to integrate (Attitude), cultural similarity (Identity), and responsibility for their migration (Control) were more likely to find discrimination acceptable, while those prioritizing migrants' societal contributions (Reciprocity) were more resistant to discrimination across all domains. Intergroup contact mattered selectively: frequency had no effect, while contact quality consistently predicted lower acceptance and moderated several deservingness effects. These patterns reveal conditional rather than categorical commitments to equality, with support granted on perceived merit, gratitude, or compatibility. Discrimination thus reflects not only failed tolerance but moral reasoning that treats fairness as something migrants must earn. items.title: Why Liberalism Might Last
items.affiliation: HOGENT University of Applied Sciences and Arts; Ghent University; Ghent University Hospital

extra.summary: ABSTRACT In ‘Can Liberalism Last?’ Anomaly and Faria (2023) argue that liberal societies tend to undermine their own long‐term survival, chiefly by fostering conditions—urbanization, mass migration from culturally distant regions and sub‐replacement fertility—that erode social trust and grant a demographic advantage to illiberal groups, whereas liberalism's philosophical commitments bar the corrective measures (immigration restriction, pronatalism, nation‐building) that non‐liberal states can freely deploy. In this commentary we grant that these challenges are real, but argue that the inference from demographic trends to liberalism's collapse is too pessimistic. We identify five mechanisms that could counteract these trends. First, the fertility advantage of illiberal groups assumes high intergenerational retention, yet defection is pervasive and can accelerate suddenly once preference falsification and pluralistic ignorance give way. Second, liberal states are increasingly willing to adopt migration restrictions and pronatalist policies and—contrary to what Anomaly and Faria contend—such measures need not violate core liberal principles. Third, the economic and technological superiority of open societies allows them to exert outsized global influence. Fourth, because illiberal groups tend to be more resistant to change, some of their traits may become maladaptive as conditions change. items.title: The Enemy Who Never Went Away: Memory, Nationalism and China's Japan Policy During the Cold War
items.affiliation: Birmingham City University; University College Birmingham; University of Birmingham

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This study reassesses the relationship between war memory, nationalism and Sino–Japanese relations during the Cold War. Contrary to the dominant view in existing scholarship that China's nationalist remembering of the war emerged during the 1980s and 1990s, this article, drawing on an extensive survey of the People's Daily , demonstrates that war memory was actively employed in China's foreign policy discourse on Japan from 1949 to 1972. It challenges the ‘collective amnesia’ and ‘communism‐over‐nationalism’ theses by showing that foreign policy discourse functioned as a key arena for the production of memory and nationalist narratives during the Mao era. It contributes to the literature by uncovering a long‐neglected side of memory, nationalism and Sino–Japanese relations.

items.title: What Is ‘African Music’? Musical Categorization and Nation Building in Post‐Colonial Mozambique

extra.summary: ABSTRACT What is meant by ‘African music’ in a newly independent African country, and who holds the authority to define it? Focusing on Mozambique after independence, this article examines how musical categorization became a central political and ideological concern within FRELIMO's nation‐building project. Through an analysis of a highly polarized public debate surrounding the musical programming of the national radio station (1981), this article argues that music functioned not only as a vehicle for promoting revolutionary values but also as a contested site where racialized, territorial and historical imaginaries of ‘Africanness’ were negotiated. Drawing on an ‘ethnography of the past’, combining archival analysis of listeners' letters with interviews with key radio workers and cultural agents, this study situates these debates within broader discussions on nation‐building and musical categorization. Ultimately, it demonstrates how disputes over ‘African music’ both reflected unresolved issues in FRELIMO's history, while foreshadowing changes that would only materialize in later years.

items.title: Nationalism and Education in the Arctic: A Study of Greenland in the Context of the Kingdom of Denmark
items.affiliation: University of Copenhagen; IT University of Copenhagen; Ilisimatusarfik

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article analyses the coconstitution of nationalism and education in Greenland ( Kalaallit Nunaat ) within the Kingdom of Denmark. Drawing on Ernest Gellner, Benedict Anderson, Michael Billig and Siniša Malešević, it argues that schooling standardises language, history and civic repertoires, thereby fabricating the modern national subject. Situated in a postcolonial and settler‐colonial context, the analysis traces Greenland's trajectory from its status as a Danish‐led colony—a period during which Greenland was relatively isolated (1721–1953)—through county status and assimilation (1953–1979), to Greenlandisation under Home Rule from 1979 and Self‐Government from 2009. Despite linguistic reorientation in recent decades, a de facto hierarchy persists: Danish remains the principal medium of upper secondary education and a vector of social mobility. Against the backdrop of demographic decline and geopolitical intensification, the article contends that Arctic sovereignty is best conceived as multilayered and interdependent and that education is pivotal to nation formation and capacity building, irrespective of future constitutional choices.

items.title: Imagining a Nation: A Social Representation Analysis of the ‘Idea of India’ in Contemporary Times

extra.summary: ABSTRACT The present research explored how different age cohorts conceptualize the ‘Idea of India’ through the lens of the social representations theory (SRT). Data were collected for three age cohorts—young adults (18–24 years), working adults (25–50 years) and older adults (50 + years). In total, 300 participants were asked to perform a free association task, in which they provided five spontaneous ideas relating to India. Analysis using the structural approach was used as well as prototypical analysis to reveal both common core items and unique peripheral representations between generational groups. Findings showed a shared aspirational core across generations, with national prestige, modernization, social justice and cultural appreciation as the core concerns. There were, however, notable inter‐generational differences in both central and peripheral representational themes. Young adults stressed technological progress and international positioning, working adults economic progress and institutional solidity and older adults historical continuity and traditional values. This research contributes three important findings: (1) It presents exploratory evidence, within an urban middleclass sample from two Indian cities, of how national identity may be both shared and differentially constructed across age cohorts; (2) it illustrates the value of prototypical analysis in charting changing social representations of nationhood; and (3) it identifies particular points of convergenc

items.title: Welfare and ethnic boundary deactivation in left-wing nationalist mobilization
items.affiliation: Universidade de Santiago de Compostela; Universidade da Coruña

extra.summary: Why do left-wing substate nationalist parties increasingly prioritize welfare-centered over ethnonationalist appeals? While existing research has documented the growing prominence of socioeconomic issues in nationalist politics, the strategic advantages that welfare frames offer for nationalist mobilization remain overlooked. Drawing on scholarship on ethnic boundary-making and framing theory, this article addresses this gap through an analysis of Bloque Nacionalista Galego (BNG), one of Spain’s fastest-growing nationalist parties. Using a multi-source corpus, we employ the notion of ethnic boundary deactivation to analyze how nationalist elites strategically shift the political frontier away from ethnocultural distinctions and toward welfare-centered frames across different stages of political competition. The findings show that Galician nationalism continues to rely on a distinct ethnocultural conception of the nation, yet strategically prioritizes welfare-centered frames when seeking to mobilize support. First, welfare allows nationalist actors to articulate a positive, forward-looking national project that displaces the imagery of resistance and grievance commonly associated with ethnocultural claims. Second, welfare creates a new political frontier organized around the defense of national interests, subordinating ethnocultural markers to welfare goals. Third, it anchors mobilization in an emotional regime of hope and collective solidarity that reinforces collective actio

items.title: ‘They don’t want us here’: Reworking neighbourhood nationalism in post-Southport England

extra.summary: From mid-July 2025, an organised nationalist movement known as Operation Raise the Colours (ORC) began saturating English residential streets with St George’s Cross and Union Jack flags. Emerging one year after the Southport riots of summer 2024, ORC has converted lampposts, roundabouts and motorway bridges into a communicative grid that addresses certain bodies as out of place. This article asks how young people read, feel, and navigate this transformation. Drawing on three gender-specific focus groups and eight follow-up interviews with twenty-two participants aged 18–25, conducted between December 2025 and February 2026, the article advances three theoretical claims that together constitute a structural reworking of Les Back’s concept of ‘neighbourhood nationalism’. Where Back’s 1996 South London ethnography found neighbourhood-scale belonging to be sometimes hybrid and inclusive, ORC’s neighbourhood nationalism is durably exclusionary, deliberately engineered, and distinctly gendered. Empirical analysis develops these claims through the strategic translation of radical-right symbolism into mainstream patriotic respectability, the relational damage of flag-saturation among proximate neighbours, and the embodied risk-calibration practices that Muslim women perform in saturated streets. The article extends Mirza’s embodied intersectionality from a narratological into a territorial register and Mondon’s mainstreaming framework from discourse into space.

items.title: From diaspora to neighbourhood: Reconfiguring diasporic engagement through intra-diasporic solidarities among immigrant mothers in Quebec
items.affiliation: Nipissing University; Saint Paul University; Carleton University

extra.summary: This article examines the reconfiguration of diasporic engagement through everyday practices of immigrant mothers in Quebec. While previous scholarship on diaspora and diasporic philanthropy has focused on transnational flows, remittances, and formal organizations, this study highlights localized and relational forms of engagement within the host societies. Drawing on 20 qualitative interviews and 11 observations of immigrant mothers in Quebec, the analysis identifies four interconnected forms of diasporic engagement: intra-diasporic mutual aid, cultural transmission, informal community mediation, and transnational family care. Guided by feminist care theory and scholarship on social reproduction, the findings indicate that motherhood constitutes a central tenet for organizing solidarities, reproducing identities, and sustaining support networks across both local and transnational contexts. The article argues that immigrant mothers serve as micro-social infrastructures of diaspora, linking family, community, and neighbourhood lives. This perspective expands prevailing understandings of diasporic engagement as gendered, selective, and relational phenomenon embedded in everyday care practices.

items.title: What is migration populism? Concept development and the Italian case
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: This paper proposes the concept of migration populism to address the analytical ambiguity surrounding the relationship between populism and migration in current public and academic debates. Building on the ideational approach, it defines migration populism as the framing of migration issues produced within broader populist ideologies, particularly-though not exclusively-by populist radical right parties. It identifies three core elements: a thin interpretation of migration that flexibly incorporates elements drawn from complementary ideologies such as nationalism and nativism; an alarmist narrative portraying pro-migration elites as betraying the "pure people"; and the attribution of policy failure to liberal-democratic constraints. To demonstrate the analytical value and explanatory power of this conceptualisation, the paper analyses the Italian case, showing how these elements converge within a specific political and institutional context. It concludes by reflecting on the benefits of a clearly delimited concept for comparative research.

items.title: Serial diasporas : how emigrating gulf noncitizens evolve into new diasporas
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
items.affiliation: University of California, Irvine; University of London; Gulf Research Center; SOAS University of London

extra.summary: How do diaspora identities and engagements transform when migrants emigrate after long-term residence from a site of protracted noncitizenship? Unlike Global South-rooted communities in Euro-American contexts, whose diasporic identities are historically understood through citizenship, settlement, and mobility, Gulf-based South and Southeast Asians inhabit an order structured by serial migration, legal precarity, and noncitizenship. Drawing on 23 life-story interviews in English, Hindi, and Filipino with long-term resident Indian and Filipino nationals emigrating from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), we theorise serial diasporas – noncitizen groups with a diasporic homeland outside state formation, ethnicity, or nationality. In the Gulf, we argue that the emergence of serial diaspora is a byproduct of long-term homemaking practices and transnational belonging amid protracted noncitizenship and serial migration. We sketch three illustrative sub-types of serial diasporas – ambivalent, cosmopolitan, and entrepreneurial – each engaged in increasing levels of sociopolitical claims-making and Gulf-centric community formation abroad. Ultimately, we advance diaspora and migration debates by featuring the emergence of serial diasporas and retheorising diaspora ‘origins’, ethnicity, and claims-making in contemporary South-South migration-centric contexts.

items.title: Making diversity policies under political pressure
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: Critical diversity studies claim that diversity policies are often devoid of meaning – which is said to impede the efficacy of these policies for social justice. This alleged meaninglessness, however, is rarely treated as the result of bureaucrats’ affective imaginations of these policies. We know little about the feelings of bureaucrats that precede diversity’s discursive meaninglessness and about reluctance to act as a result of specific political imaginations. This article studies politically sensitive forms of manoeuvring that emerge in bureaucrats’ attempts to ‘safeguard’ diversity within municipal policy to make it ‘sustainable’ in a time of (far) right-wing upsurge. These forms of manoeuvring lead my inquiry into the ‘institutional work’ that diversity workers engage in across changing political tides. By following the process of making a particular diversity document in a Dutch city administration in the middle of a right-wing-voting rural area, I add ethnographic detail to studies on coping mechanisms of bureaucrats faced with political pressure. In showing how bureaucrats affectively imagine diversity policies – in retrospect, in the present, and into the future – I argue that backlash against diversity asks for new analytic tools to grasp the changing politically prefigurative meanings of what diversity policies were, are, and could be.
