items.title: Side-stepping stigma: accessing labour market opportunities in superdiverse cities
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: This article examines strategies employed by first- and second-generation migrant youth to navigate employment discrimination in three superdiverse cities: Melbourne (Australia), Birmingham (United Kingdom) and Toronto (Canada). Drawing on 119 interviews conducted between 2019 and early 2020, it explores how young people from migrant backgrounds perceive and respond to biased hiring practices. Three key themes are discussed: awareness of conscious and unconscious employer bias; strategic use of intragroup networks for initial labour market entry and skill development; and adaptive ‘covering’ behaviours including consciously altering communication styles, appearance, and cultural interests to gain acceptance in majority group-dominated workplaces. The study challenges deficit-based narratives that characterise minority community networks as providing ‘low’ social capital, instead demonstrating their potential for providing protective and developmental spaces. While participants exhibited agency in developing transcultural capital to navigate discriminatory environments, structural barriers persist despite individual adaptive strategies. The research contributes to understanding how marginalised youth negotiate exclusionary labour markets while highlighting the continued reality of systemic discrimination for career progression.

items.title: The geography of immigrants in same-sex couples in the United States
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: The policy landscape for same-sex couples in the United States has changed rapidly in recent years, and the number of immigrants in same-sex couples has markedly increased. Little is known, however, about where these lesbian, gay, bisexual, and queer (LGBQ) immigrants settle and experience these shifting policy environments. Using American Community Survey data from 2008–2023 and original datasets, this paper studies the geographic context of immigrants in same-sex cohabiting couples in the U.S., comparing them to immigrants in different-sex couples and the U.S.-born in same-sex couples. We find that the distribution of immigrants in same-sex couples is expanding across the U.S. over time. Individually, these immigrants resemble U.S.-born LGBQ Americans, with higher incomes and educational attainment. At the geographic level, they appear more distinct, clustering in areas with more LGBTQ+ nonprofit organisations, greater numbers of immigrants, higher density, and higher property values than the areas where straight immigrants or the U.S.-born in same-sex couples tend to live. Our findings contribute to a fuller understanding of this rapidly growing population and its unique characteristics.

items.title: Displaced citizenship: war-driven political action and temporalities of displacement among Ukrainians
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 led to the displacement of millions of people, many of whom fled abroad, grappling with survivor guilt and seeking ways to remain part of Ukraine’s fight. Based on ethnographic fieldwork with displaced Ukrainians in Prague, this article examines their war-related political activism, emphasising the immediacy of displacement, the war-intensified sense of diasporic responsibility, and the uncertainty of temporary protection. It situates their engagement within the relational landscape of the receiving society, where displaced persons negotiated political voice and recognition amid experiences of othering and self-imposed restrictions on political action as non-citizens. To capture these dynamics, the article develops the analytical lens of displaced citizenship. Rather than approaching displacement as a background condition, displaced citizenship foregrounds how urgency, rupture, and uncertainty become constitutive of political subjectivity. It shows how the immediacy of forced movement, grief, separation, and enduring concerns for those left behind generate moral and political obligations, while uncertainty about protection, return, emplacement, and societal reception shapes how displaced persons navigate political action in receiving societies. In doing so, the article contributes to debates on migration, citizenship, and political participation by recentring the temporalities of displacement in the study of political engagement

items.title: Exclusive capital: how Ghanaian return migrants value dual citizenship
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
items.affiliation: University of Oxford; European University Institute

extra.summary: Dual citizenship is known to come with socio-economic benefits, particularly for migrants from the Global South who naturalise in a country of the Global North. This paper explores the ways in which these socio-economic benefits are portable to the Global South when migrants return. Investigating the case of Ghanaian voluntary return migration, it asks: What are the socio-economic benefits of dual citizenship for returnees’ everyday life after return? Building on 49 qualitative interviews with voluntary returnees, it finds that dual citizenship is perceived to offer substantive benefits to returnees’ lives in Ghana. These benefits go well beyond offering an ‘exit strategy’ and are best described as Bourdieusian (economic, social, and cultural) capital that can be derived from citizenship in the Global North but largely relies on its combination with Ghanaian citizenship. One group of returnees stood out by not seeing any additional socio-economic value in dual citizenship for life in Ghana: members of politically well-connected families of Ghana’s elite. The paper concludes that dual citizenship matters in more ways than previously acknowledged, as the case of Ghana points to an under-recognised socio-economic mobility mechanism through return migration with dual citizenship.

items.title: Transnational social protection in East and Southeast Asia: resources, restrictions, and risks
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
items.affiliation: Villanova University; Wellesley College; National Taiwan University

extra.summary: This introduction provides a conceptual map of how systems of social protection and cross-border migration influence one another across East and Southeast Asia and beyond. Much of the literature on Transnational Social Protection (TSP) focuses on the (in)ability of migrants in Europe, the United States, and parts of Latin America to protect themselves and their families. With some notable exceptions, few scholars have explored these questions in the Asian context, where modernisation processes, social and political structures, and belief systems differ starkly from those in the West. This introduction examines how the politics, policies, and practices of sending and receiving states uniquely shape migrants’ access to rights and protections in the region. We also discuss the roles that market, third-sector institutions, and personal networks play in supporting migrants and their families. Taken together, the articles in this volume showcase how migrants construct resource environments across national borders in response to the unique opportunities and constraints afforded by the Asian context, compare responses of sending and receiving country states, and propose directions for future research.

items.title: Stabilising emotion, structuring aspiration: Taiwanese language coaching as pre-migration protection
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: In an age of competitive global higher education, how do international students develop and maintain the confidence to pursue their ambitions of studying abroad? Existing research emphasises the role of language coaching centres in preparing students for international admissions exams (e.g. TOEFL, GRE) but has paid little attention to the emotional dimensions of pre-migration preparation. Drawing on four years of ethnographic fieldwork in Taiwanese language coaching centres and a content analysis of related online forums, I demonstrate that, in addition to transmitting content knowledge and test-taking strategies, these coaching centres play a crucial role in managing student anxiety. Specifically, I show how (1) environmental, (2) instructional, and (3) interpersonal elements of the coaching centres mitigate anxiety and promote a vision of attainable success by fostering a sense of cultural familiarity, personal control, and community support. Extending the transnational social protection framework (TSP) to the pre-migration phase, these findings demonstrate how language coaching centres function as sites of emotional preparation for global admissions, making success in this field appear both achievable and deserved. As such, they represent crucial infrastructures of pre-migration protection.

items.title: Dyadic transnational social protection: eldercare and domestic worker migration
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
items.affiliation: National University of Singapore; National Chung Cheng University

extra.summary: This paper challenges the usual individual-focused view of social protection by introducing a care dyad framework that treats migrant domestic workers (MDWs) and their elderly employers as one analytical unit. Using Singapore as a case study, it shows that the welfare of both groups is intertwined and shaped by transnational resource environments, even though the older adults themselves are not migrants. The study argues that support for care dyads extends across borders because the employers' dependence on MDWs links their wellbeing to systems in both sending and receiving countries. It also highlights that while scholarship often centres MDWs' resource environments, a dialogical approach is needed to prioritise mutual wellbeing and recognise the shared social protection needs of both parties. The analysis also delves into the roles of state and non-state actors, including social enterprises and non-governmental organisations, in both migrant-sending and receiving countries. It highlights their potential to co-construct and expand hybrid resource environments. The limitations in state-provided social protection underscore the necessity for non-state interventions to bolster support for both MDWs and their employers, promoting a more integrated approach to transnational social protection. But the regulatory oversight of the state remains important to ensure equitable practices.

extra.summary: East Asian migration regimes are characterised by temporariness, selective incorporation and restrictive pathways to permanent settlement. items.title: Out of sight, out of mind: Italy-Libya and its colonial past and present
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: Contemporary cooperation between Italy and Libya on migration control is often analysed in a vacuum, framed as a pragmatic response to human trafficking and irregular migration. This article argues that such policies cannot be fully understood without engaging with the colonial history that continues to shape relations between the two countries. Drawing on focus group discussions, I examine how coloniality informs contemporary understandings of migration control, responsibility, and legitimacy within the Italian political sphere. I trace the historical relationship between Italy and Libya, highlighting continuities between colonial practices of internment, racialised governance, and contemporary outsourcing of migration control. Using Stoler’s concept of colonial aphasia, I explore how these forms of coloniality emerge in public discourse. I argue that coloniality shapes public understandings of Italy’s role in Libya, through colonial aphasia and paternalistic attitudes, affecting people’s understanding of responsibility to people on the move, and creating hierarchies of deservingness along racialised and neo-colonial lines. By examining the relationship between colonial memory, legitimacy, and migration governance, the article contributes to scholarship on the coloniality of migration and the enduring influence of colonial histories on contemporary border regimes.

items.title: Beyond the arena: cultural rituals and taboos in Indigenous Naga Wrestling

extra.summary: This article examines the cultural rituals and taboos associated with Indigenous Naga Wrestling (INW) and their significance in shaping social behaviour, cultural identity, and community cohesion among the Nagas. The study adopted a qualitative research design and collected primary data through in-depth interviews, participant observation, and focus group discussions with former and current wrestlers and wrestling enthusiasts. The findings show that ritual blessings, dietary observances, and ceremonial preparations enhanced wrestlers’ confidence, strength, protection, and spiritual well-being, while taboos regulated conduct, reinforced moral discipline, and strengthened collective identity. These practices also facilitated the intergenerational transmission of indigenous knowledge. The study argues that INW reflects the patriarchal structure of traditional Naga society while remaining a vital cultural institution. Although a series of ritual practices have declined because of modernization, Christianity, globalization, and shifting social values, INW continues to preserve its distinctive cultural identity and heritage.

items.title: The de facto borderland as a space of uneven ontological insecurity: insights from a village in Poonch, Jammu and Kashmir
items.affiliation: Manipal Academy of Higher Education; National Institute of Advanced Studies

extra.summary: De facto border scholarship often foregrounds territorialisation and strategic security, leaving borderlands’ lived social form underexamined. This article argues that the memory-mediated relational process through which co-located Muslim, Hindu, and Sikh residents assign different meanings to remembered Partition, militancy, and resulting displacements contributes to the lived social form of the village-level de facto borderland setting they share. The article conceptualises the non-equivalent implications of this process across residents’ mutually implicated positions as uneven ontological insecurity. This interpretivist study draws on 40 semi-structured interviews and non-participant observation in Sangli Dara, a pseudonymous village adjoining the Line of Control in Poonch, Jammu and Kashmir. Fear, anticipation, and estrangement operate as mnemonic modalities through which residents’ interpretations sustain, strain, or unsettle narrative continuity, routine familiarity, and symbolic coherence. The article advances de facto borderland scholarship by locating remembrance within lived social form and extends ontological security scholarship by theorising insecurity as internally uneven.

items.title: Purity as politics: crafting discipline in the puritan public sphere of Assam and its institutional sedimentation

extra.summary: This essay theorizes the concept of ‘puritan public sphere’ and uses it as a framework to explain the purifying nature of Assamese subnationalism in practice. It argues that linguo-cultural purity serves as a prerequisite for civic legitimacy in the state and shifts away from classical notions of the public sphere as inclusive and dialogic. The study examines how symbolic violence and moral discipline normalize the marginalization of those deemed outsiders in the state, thereby pathologizing any deviation from puritan norms. It uses Cotton University as a case study and conducts a discourse analysis of ‘Cottonian’ magazines (1978–1985), along with interviews with marginalized students, to understand how puritan values become embedded in institutional life. It distinguishes puritanism from xenophobia by demonstrating that rather than expelling difference, puritanism disciplines it. The study contributes to debates on nationalism, identity, and institutional power while advocating a more plural and agonistic public sphere.

items.title: The frontier on the front lines: the Chinese Communist discourse on China’s southwest and its peoples during the Korean War, 1950–1953
items.affiliation: University of Freiburg; Institute for Frontier Areas of Psychology and Mental Health

extra.summary: This article argues that the Korean War (1950–1953) was a discursive event through which the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) sought to buttress its vision of Chinese nationhood and territoriality within the newly-founded People’s Republic of China. It examines the CCP’s political discourse on China’s ethnoculturally-diverse southwestern borderlands and so-called ‘minority nationalities’ (shaoshu minzu) against the Korean War background. Through an analysis of People’s Daily (Renmin ribao) articles published between 1950 and 1953 that feature China’s southwestern frontier, I identify three prevalent discursive designs that connected the remote southwest to the Korean War front and endorsed a vision of a multi-nationality territorialized nation-state: (1) the military participation of minority nationalities, which exemplified a cross-nationality Chinese war effort; (2) representations of a resource-rich southwestern frontier, manifesting a geostrategic gaze on a territorialized periphery; and (3) the fight against ‘counterrevolutionaries,’ which integrated minority nationalities into narratives of national humiliation and anti-imperialist struggle.

items.title: Feminized Revival: Han Chinese Dress, Gender and Cultural Nationalism in Contemporary China

extra.summary: Abstract Women hold disproportionate authority in China’s contemporary Hanfu revival, where Han-ness operates through implicit cultural codes rather than explicit ethnic claims. Recent scholarship highlights how Han-ness circulates as a moral, etiquette-centred grammar of “proper culture.” Drawing on 18 months of ethnography across six sites in China, this article shows how gender mediates that grammar and shapes the performances of Han-ness. Women, as arbiters of taste and propriety, enact an assertive banal nationalism through aesthetic and organizational labour. Men, marginal within the field, perform defensive overt nationalism through didactic historical narratives and moralized claims to legitimacy. To explain this pattern of identity formation and boundary making, I advance the notion of gendered everyday nationhood. The article contributes to scholarship on nationalism by showing how embodied practices sustain national belonging, and how mundane evaluation and boundary policing reproduce nationhood in everyday life.

items.title: Social Work on the China-Myanmar Border: State-NGO Synchronization

extra.summary: This article investigates the evolving relationship between the Chinese state and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) through the case of Ruili, a county-level city on the China-Myanmar frontier. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork, interviews, and extensive archival records, we develop an analytical framework of synchronization for the Chinese state and NGOs to capture how the relationship between them has changed. The analysis identifies four stages: a compensatory phase, in which foreign NGOs filled governance gaps and nurtured local capacity; a parallel growth phase, in which domestic NGOs and local governments expanded activities together; an alignment phase, in which NGOs reoriented themselves to implement national strategies such as rural revitalization and public health security; and a global outreach phase, in which selected NGOs extended their services abroad within the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). We present a case in which a welfare NGO working on cross-border social problems developed its operations alongside local state agencies. This article contributes to current debates on the adaptation of Chinese NGOs to a new environment by showing how coproduction, strategic alignment, and bounded negotiation have unfolded over time in a politically sensitive frontier setting.

items.title: Embeddedness Under Fire: How Chinese Private Firms Navigate Conflict Risks in Northern Myanmar

extra.summary: As one of Myanmar’s largest sources of foreign investment, China has been exposed to the civil war that intensified after the 2021 coup. Drawing on a mixed embeddedness perspective and interview-based fieldwork, this article examines how Chinese private firms operate in Myanmar’s conflict-affected regions without formal state protection or legal guarantees. It argues that their resilience rests on embedding commercial activity within fragmented governance. Institutionally, firms align with non-state armed authorities, adapt across shifting jurisdictions, and benefit from protective norms tied to Chinese identity. Socially, they mobilize ethnic and kinship ties, intermediaries, and localized information networks. These mechanisms, though costly and imperfect, convert unstable environments into workable orders. The article contributes to Global China scholarship by foregrounding private enterprises as adaptive actors in conflict settings.

items.title: The Virtue of Bias? China’s Stakeholder Mediation in the Iran and North Korea Nuclear Crises
items.affiliation: Peking University; Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies

extra.summary: Why does China mediate differently across similar security crises? Challenging mediation theory’s neutrality assumption, this article conceptualises ‘stakeholder mediation’ as engagement by third parties whose security, economic, or reputational interests are exposed to a conflict’s outcome. Such mediators hold leverage but risk entrapment and reputational costs. Using a most-similar design, process tracing, diplomat memoirs, declassified documents, and elite interviews, we examine China’s role in the North Korean and Iranian nuclear crises. Despite structural similarities, China adopted markedly different postures. Variation in stake exposure shapes risk calculations, entry timing, and leverage strategies: high immediate security stakes in Korea raised China’s intervention threshold through entrapment fears, whereas economic and reputational stakes in Iran lowered the risks of early multilateral engagement, while US–China relations operated as a scope condition.

items.title: Stratified regulation: unpacking value alignment of Chinese LLMs

extra.summary: While previous studies examine how biases in training data and models shape LLMs’ values, less attention has been paid to how political orientations vary across different deployment modes. This paper proposes a stratified regulation framework, arguing that the Chinese government balances technological innovation with information regulation. Cloud-based models, accessible to the public, are strictly regulated to ensure ideological security, whereas local deployments face relaxed restrictions to facilitate innovation. Using 100 ideological prompts and stance analysis, the paper examines how information regulation affects DeepSeek R1 in local versus cloud contexts. The results reveal that locally deployed models display more diverse perspectives, while the cloud versions exhibit a pronounced ideologically positive orientation, reflecting real-time alignment and official-tone templates. English prompts elicit more critical responses, whereas Chinese prompts produce more political rightness content. These findings demonstrate a stratified regulatory approach: broad training-phase filtering across all deployments and real-time alignment for cloud models. This study is the first to document the value differences across different deployment contexts, providing methods and data to quantify LLM regulation and advance the understanding of technological governance in China.

items.title: Upskilling and lowered risks of AI-labor substitution: the impact of the National College Entrance Exam reform in China
items.affiliation: Fudan University; Tsinghua University; Peking University; EA Technology

extra.summary: Can education shield graduates from the storm of AI-induced displacement in the labor market? To address this research question, the study uses China’s National College Entrance Examination reform as a policy shock and examines how the abolition of the liberal arts–science tracking system affects graduates’ labor market outcomes. Following the upskilling framework and employing a cohort difference-in-differences research design, this study finds that graduates exposed to the National College Entrance Exam reform are more likely to secure an occupation with lower risks of AI-labor substitution, despite the reform not being designed to achieve this spillover effect. Further analyses reveal that this enhanced resilience stems from graduates sorting into occupations that demand higher levels of transferable abilities and work styles, competencies which remain less susceptible to AI-labor substitution. Operational skills are not one of the mediating skills because they are highly vulnerable to the displacement. The findings suggest that interdisciplinary training can endow students with skills irreplaceable in China’s AI-oriented labor market. Moreover, this benefit is more pronounced among students from high-income families than their counterparts from low-income families. Educational policies should be recalibrated to align with the context of rapid AI transformation.

extra.summary: Abstract: This study aims to analyze the development of county-level Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) services in Guangxi based on grounded theory, providing theoretical support for proposing corresponding countermeasures to promote the development of TCM services in Guangxi counties. We highlight how this approach can help examine not only the discursive connections among far-right movements but also the novel geopolitical visions and transformations that underlie them. extra.summary: This paper examines the hybrid institutional arrangements governing water security in post-conflict South Sudan. Based on a qualitative comparative case study of two sub-national states, it analyses how formal state agencies, customary authorities, and non-governmental organisations negotiate authority over water resources in practice. The findings reveal a landscape where customary systems, led by chiefs and water custodians, exercise primary de facto control over access and management, often operating in parallel to or in tension with a weak formal state apparatus. This hybridity manifests in both collaborative and conflictual interactions, directly shaping—and often entrenching—differentiated access along social and ethnic lines. Theoretically, the study advances the concept of hybrid governance by demonstrating how these emergent systems critically determine the delivery of an essential resource, moving analysis beyond a narrow focus on political or security institutions. It concludes that water governance serves as a microcosm of South Sudan's contested statebuilding, where multiple sources of legitimacy coexist. For policymakers, the analysis underscores the necessity of engaging constructively with existing hybrid orders rather than imposing external, state-centric blueprints.

extra.summary: The rising burden of abdominal obesity (AO) has emerged as a significant global public health concern. items.title: Religious Ethos and Political Discourse: A Comparative Analysis of the Role of Religion in Shaping the National Ideologies of Japan and Singapore

extra.summary: Abstract The purpose of the present study was to identify the mechanisms of the functioning of religious ethos in the political discourse of Japan and Singapore. The findings showed that Japan developed a distinctive model of religious-political interaction based on Shintoism as a sacralised foundation of statehood. During the Meiji period, State Shinto legitimised political authority and national unity, while after 1945, religious symbols continued to influence national consciousness despite official secularism. extra.summary: Abstract INTRODUCTION: Research on the potential role of cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) as risk factors for Lewy body dementia (LBD) is limited, and findings from existing studies remain inconclusive. items.affiliation: Université Bordeaux Montaigne; Sciences, Philosophie, Humanités

extra.summary: Do large language models (LLMs) possess a measurable "personality," and how do the linguistic properties of training corpora shape their cognitive style and downstream reasoning? This paper approaches these questions from a sociolinguistic perspective on machine "identity." This manuscript is positioned explicitly as a conceptual perspective paper: it does not present original experimental data, nor does it constitute a systematic review with defined search strategies or inclusion criteria. Instead, it synthesises key published findings into two original theoretical frameworks intended to guide future empirical and engineering work. We examine evidence that LLMs exhibit reliable, valid Big Five personality traits—particularly in large, instruction-tuned models—and that continued pre-training on domain-specific corpora may shape those traits through measurable linguistic features: imperative ratio, type-token ratio (TTR), and syntactic complexity. We then analyse how standard-language ideology embedded in training corpora is amplified in model outputs, disadvantaging dialect and minority-language communities. Building on these findings, we propose two conceptual contributions: (1) a Personality Engineering (PE) framework for targeted continued pre-training to cultivate task-appropriate cognitive profiles, and (2) a Language Ideology Propagation Model (LIPM) mapping the pipeline from corpus composition to societal impact. items.title: Borrowed Shame: Hao Hongmei as a Narrative Resource for Sun Shaoping's Moral Image

extra.summary: This article reconsiders one of the most frequently moralized episodes in Lu Yao's Ordinary World: Hao Hongmei's theft of handkerchiefs at the end of high school and Sun Shaoping's intervention on her behalf. Existing readings often treat the incident as evidence of Hao's vanity, compromised character, or eventual moral education. Such interpretations remain too close to the evaluative grammar supplied by the novel itself. Through close reading informed by affect theory, the anthropology of the gift, class analysis, and rhetorical narrative ethics, this article argues that the episode organizes a transfer of moral value. Hao's shame originates in a social relation. Graduation gifts impose a debt of reciprocity on a student whose poverty has to remain concealed if she is to preserve ordinary membership in the class. Once she is caught, however, the narrative reallocates agency and interpretive authority. Sun explains her motives, pays for the handkerchiefs, controls the circulation of knowledge, and converts the objects from evidence of theft into gifts that can safely re-enter social exchange. Witnesses then ratify his kindness, while Hao is reduced largely to fear, tears, and gratitude. Her crisis therefore becomes the condition under which Sun's goodness can appear as exceptional, magnanimous, and independent of romantic self-interest. I call this process borrowed shame: the narrative conversion of one character's socially produced humiliation into another character's ethic

extra.summary: Abstract: This study explores the ethical dimensions of worker precarity and protest agency in the context of ongoing polycrisis conditions in Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan. Drawing upon publicly available protest videos from various occupational groups-such as healthcare, education, and public sector employees-the study employs a thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns of ethical discourse, institutional critique, and collective resistance. A total of six protest cases were analyzed. The findings reveal six overarching ethical themes: precarity and vulnerability, moral agency and resistance, institutional betrayal, collective dignity and solidarity, justice-oriented appeals, and emotional exhaustion. These themes reflect how workers’ lived experiences are morally constructed and publicly articulated as demands for justice, recognition, and accountability. Radar diagrams further quantify the relative intensity of each theme across protest categories. The results suggest that workers do not merely react to material deprivation but frame their struggles through ethical language and civic engagement, thereby demonstrating moral resilience amid systemic neglect. This study contributes to the literature on business ethics, worker agency, and crisis governance by highlighting how ethical imagination and protest narratives are mobilized from the margins in response to institutional failures. extra.summary: Australia’s domestic market for elephant (Elephantidae ssp.) ivory remains active online, despite long-standing international controls and pledges to close domestic trade. We conducted snapshot monitoring of surface-web vendors (online auction houses and webstores with ‘buy-it-now’ payment options) and a survey of Facebook Marketplace posts made between January and June 2025, sampled every two weeks. items.title: Eating escargot: seasonal terrestrial gastropod exploitation by forest foragers in the ethnoarchaeological record of Central Africa

extra.summary: Abstract In the prehistoric record, the presence of small-sized resources including gastropods is often viewed as a marker of increased dietary breadth, declining foraging efficiency and/or flexible subsistence patterns involving diversified foraging activities. However, researchers often find it difficult to distinguish natural gastropod accumulations from those created by anthropogenic processes. Here we report on the context, profitability and methods of the seasonal hand-collecting and processing of terrestrial gastropods based on the observations of contemporary Central African forest foragers. In this context, gastropods were exploited in response to temporary and seasonal reductions in the availability of meat and changes in labor demands that allowed women and children to engage in this activity. Analyses of faunal remains from a wet season encampment presented here shows how different kinds of gastropod processing are reflected in the ethnoarchaeological record. These analyses validate several of the characteristics currently used by archaeologists to identify anthropogenic gastropod assemblages. Overall, the degree of burning, specimen completeness, and spatial distribution of snail shells parallels that of other small-sized fauna. Some characteristics, such as shell completeness and spatial association, can reflect different preparation techniques that, in this case, may be indicators of ethnic identity and site clean-up activities. items.title: Braiding African Indigenous Education and Western Knowledge: A Case Study In Strengthening Cultural Identity

extra.summary: This article investigates why braiding African Indigenous Education (AIE) and Western education is critical to the preservation of African cultural identity. It first defines AIE and then traces its historical disruption through missionary, colonial, apartheid, and post-independence educational models. Drawing on case studies from Namibia’s educational system, the analysis illustrates the marginalization of Indigenous knowledge alongside efforts to braid it with formal schooling. Together, these cases demonstrate the need for a shift away from privileging Western knowledge as universally applicable and superior toward embracing a broader set of epistemologies, ontologies, and educational values. Incorporating AIE–particularly through experiential learning, Indigenous-language instruction, and the cultivation of culturally competent faculties–can, in turn, foster more effective community participation, critical consciousness, and cultural pride. It also explores the compatibility of modernization and globalization with Indigenous education, as evidenced by youth-led reinterpretations of tradition, and the necessity of such contemporary adaptation to AIE’s survival. This study is significant because it offers pathways for addressing systemic inequities in African education, especially those produced by colonial legacies of stigma and cultural alienation, while remaining applicable to wider global debates about curriculum and pedagogical reform and educational equity. .

items.title: The Risen Christ is the Resisting Christ: Christology in Postcolonial Africa

extra.summary: Abstract This article proposes the image of the Resisting Christ in response to African contexts marked by coloniality, dispossession, and enduring structures of domination. This image emphasizes every detail of Jesus's life, from incarnation to crucifixion, as resistance against the structures of sin operative in his time, while the resurrection functions as divine vindication of Jesus's life, teaching, and even anthropological vision. Because the African continent's ongoing entanglement in what is known as the colonial power matrix is often ignored or paid only passing attention in the forging of Christological models, the absence of the image of the Resisting Christ is worrying, although not surprising. Grounded in the theology of the incarnation and baptism, on the one hand, and an engagement with African history and literature on the other hand, the Resisting Christ, as a Christological model affirms African agency and hope, while calling for greater awareness of the nature of Africa's problems and urgency in the ongoing struggle against coloniality and its necropolitical power.

What Can 150 Years of Census Data Tell Us About Population Impacts from Extreme Weather in Sparsely Populated Northern Australia?
items.source: International Journal of Disaster Risk Science
items.affiliation: Charles Darwin University; Geographical Institute; HUN-REN Research Centre for Astronomy and Earth Sciences; Kalgoorlie Consolidated Gold Mines (Australia)

extra.summary: Abstract Populations in sparsely populated areas are vulnerable to external shocks due to limited proximal infrastructure and low adaptive capacity. In Northern Australia, and for other sparsely populated areas where human habitation is at the “edge” and attracting and retaining people is a challenge, extreme weather events are commonplace. In this study we analyze historical population and hazard data for Northern Australia to identify and profile the scale of population loss across settlement types from extreme weather events. Understanding and charting how past events have impacted the population numbers of settlements in sparsely populated areas is vital for identifying future economic, demographic, and social impacts under climate change. We found that impacts differ according to the type of settlement and hazard, with larger and more economically diversified settlements impacted primarily by floods and cyclones. Findings in this study provide practical insights into the use of census and hazard data to inform more effective and locally tailored policy and planning strategies for disaster mitigation and climate change adaptation for settlements across Northern Australia.

extra.summary: Abstract Objectives Congenital intraabdominal adhesions are fibrous ligaments that extend from the large bowel to the abdominal wall. Ladd's band is a type of congenital intraabdominal adhesions which may develop during abnormal intestinal rotation during embryonic period and lead to small bowel obstruction. Some studies suggest that dysregulated expression of some genes (CDX1, SHH, IHH) and their proteins may be associated with development of Ladd's band. Materials and Methods Specimens of 10 patients with Ladd’s band obtained during the first adhesion removal surgery were analyzed. The material of 8 patients obtained from processus vaginalis peritonei during inguinal hernia plastic served as controls. Gene (CDX1, IHH, SHH) expression was analyzed using in situ hybridization method and their proteins—using immunohistochemistry. Semi-quantitative method was used for positive cell count. Relationships between factors were analyzed using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. Results CDX1 protein was detected in similar number of fibroblasts, endotheliocytes, macrophages and mesotheliocytes of patients and control groups. CDX1 gene was expressed just in some fibroblasts. SHH protein appeared in increased number of fibroblasts, endotheliocytes, macrophages and mesotheliocytes of patients. The same gene was expressed just in some fibroblasts and endotheliocytes. Also, IHH gene positive structures appeared in similar number of different cell types in patients and control groups.

extra.summary: The increase in frequency and popularity of interdisciplinary programs at colleges and universities have led to an increased need for successful assessment models for these unique programs. items.affiliation: Pennsylvania State University; University of Chicago; Drexel University

extra.summary: The paired fins of stem tetrapods (tetrapodomorphs) have been studied extensively to understand both the phylogenetic framework of early tetrapods and the functional context of the fin-to-limb transition. Attention has predominantly been focused on a few exemplar taxa with well-preserved pectoral fins, and macroevolutionary investigations on individual fin elements have, thus far, focused solely on the humerus. Here we present new isolated pectoral fin material (NUFV 1593) from the Late Devonian of Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada that we identify as likely belonging to an elpistostegalian tetrapodomorph. NUFV 1593 is characterized by a slender, triangular radius and an intermedium with a prominent ventral groove, resembling features known from its contemporary Tiktaalik roseae. Geometric morphometric analyses of tetrapodomorph radii placed NUFV 1593 in a region of morphospace populated by elpistostegalians. However, the anatomy of NUFV 1593 shows a combination of distinctive features that we cannot attribute to any existing taxon. Differences include the relative proportions of the radius and intermedium, and the number of fin rays. Notably, the radius bears a bean-shaped proximal articular facet that is slender and dorsoventrally narrower than the rounded facets of described tetrapodomorphs, implying a movement pattern at the humeroradial joint not previously observed within the clade. items.title: Peer comparisons and the cost of pro-social behavior: Evidence from the lab
items.affiliation: University of Wyoming; CICERO Center for International Climate Research; Appalachian State University

extra.summary: Behavioral nudges in the form of peer-comparison information have, in many cases, proven effective in promoting pro-social behavior. The most prominent example is the use of home energy reports in electricity markets. While there is evidence that peer comparisons can induce reductions in externality-generating consumption, it is not clear through which channels the nudges operate. One possible channel is pecuniary: peer comparisons may make consumption choices more salient and prompt discovery of opportunities for financial savings. The other is non-pecuniary: peer comparisons may trigger moral motives such as guilt, social conformism, or social competitiveness. This study uses a controlled posted-price market experiment with externalities. We eliminate the “discovery” channel present in field settings by making financial incentives fixed and known. The experiment thus controls the pecuniary channel, leaving only the non-pecuniary, “moral” channel. We find that the nudge still enhances pro-social behavior, pointing to the moral channel’s importance. Two additional findings are that the nudge is equally effective across the treatments with low and high market prices (indicating that nudges and financial incentives neither complement nor crowd each other out) and that the nudge is more effective for participants with relatively cooperative worldviews.

items.title: The Emergence of Pottery in Southern Iran: Evidence from the Neolithic Site of Tol-e Sangi
items.affiliation: Samarkand State University named after Sharof Rashidov; University of Tourism; "Silk Road" International University of Tourism and Cultural Heritage

extra.summary: Abstract The emergence and spread of pottery production in Southwest Asia is a key topic in Neolithic archaeology, as it can provide valuable information about the technological developments and cultural changes of early societies. Archaeological excavations at the Tol-e Sangi in the Fars Cultural Zone have provided important evidence for investigating this process. Radiocarbon dates indicate that the earliest pottery in the Fars cultural zone appeared c. 6900 bc . The stratigraphic sequence of the site and the absence of any settlement hiatus between the Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) and Pottery Neolithic (PN) layers indicate that pottery emerged within a continuous local cultural tradition and not as a result of population replacement or direct adoption of a fully developed ceramic tradition. The evidence from Tol-e Sangi supports a model that considers the emergence of pottery as a result of local development within the framework of a network of regional interactions. These results demonstrate the importance of the Fars cultural region as one of the key areas for understanding the origin, adoption and development of pottery technology in Southwest Asia.

items.title: Introduction: Indexing Persons
items.affiliation: Boston College; University of Chicago; Université de Montréal

extra.summary: Abstract This article introduces the special issue, “Indexing Persons.” In this introduction, we distinguish persona- and person-indexing registers . While the former refers to speech registers that enact social types of personhood, the latter denotes registers whose indexical value enacts and points to individuated entities (social “tokens”), such as biographical persons. In so doing, we engage with the anthropological literature on the person as a cultural category, taking two complementary perspectives: a “sign’s eye view” and a “subject’s ‘I’ view.” The first view follows sign activity to ask how semiosis indexically signifies persons, while the second centers the person and asks how their subjectivity is “made up” through semiosis. Through this discussion, we introduce the articles of the issue while reflecting on the complex dialectic between these different dimensions of enregisterment and their relationship to individuation and identity, subjectivity and personhood.

items.title: Tiho’witz and the Rural Landscape: Evidence of Planned Quincunx Architecture in a Single-Period Late Classic Maya Site

extra.summary: Abstract In 2022, a lidar survey of the Three Rivers Region, conducted by the Belize Estates Archaeology Survey Team, identified multiple previously unrecorded sites, including Tiho’witz, located between and atop five hills ranging in height from 7 m to 18 m. Our 2023 ground truthing and preliminary excavations suggest that Tiho’witz is a single-period site purposely constructed with a quincunx layout during the Late Classic period. In this report, I discuss the site’s structures and main features, our initial excavation results, and the possible implications of the site’s quincunx layout.

extra.summary: Abstract We propose a virtue-based theory of ownership and governance that treats “moral ecology”—the interplay of narratives, structures, and practices—as the formative context in which virtue can develop and sustain cooperation. We argue that ownership forms and governance structures are formative ecologies that encode and teach a firm’s ends. By doing so they either cultivate or corrode the dispositions and market virtues (prudence, solidarity, reciprocity, trust) that enable cooperation. Narratives render organizational ends intelligible; structures institutionalize and authorize those ends; and practices habituate firm actors into stable dispositions over time. The mutual-insurance comparison provides the institutional context for Vanguard’s mutual ownership structure and its creation of the index fund. extra.summary: This article focuses on a technological pilot involving a digital identity system that was introduced in the hospital of a refugee camp along the Thailand-Myanmar border.
